summary: Defines a set of Diameter attribute-value pairs for describing how to classify traffic and what to do with it, such as filtering it or giving it a particular quality-of-service treatment. These building blocks can be reused by existing and future Diameter applications. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Like sticker labels for mail: one label says which letters are which, and another says what to do with them, such as rush this one or throw that one away.

subtitle: A native Diameter vocabulary for saying which traffic to match and what to do with it: filter it, shape it or mark it.

tldr.problem: Diameter used to describe packet filters and QoS as free-text rules borrowed from the FreeBSD ipfw tool, and the QoS part was underspecified.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5777 defines Diameter attribute-value pairs (AVPs) for rules. Each rule has a condition (a Classifier and optional time-of-day windows) and an action (drop, shape, mark or permit) plus QoS details.
tldr.outcome: Existing and future Diameter applications can reuse these AVPs wherever their command definitions allow. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 5777 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2010, and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. The default QoS profile it relies on is defined in RFC 5624.

sections.title: Why New Classification AVPs
sections.content:
RFC 5777 defines a set of Diameter attribute-value pairs (AVPs) for traffic classification, with actions for filtering and Quality of Service (QoS) treatment. They can be used in existing and future Diameter applications wherever the Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) of the application's command extension policy permits.

Filtering and QoS first appeared in the Diameter base protocol, RFC 3588, as the IPFilterRule and QoSFilterRule AVPs. Both used a syntax based on the FreeBSD ipfw tool, and the QoS one was underspecified until it was updated by RFC 4005.

This document replaces that free text with a uniform, extensible classification mechanism in native Diameter syntax. It adds an extensible set of actions, and it can match on Ethernet attributes such as priority bits, VLAN-IDs, LLC attributes and MAC addresses, which the old QoS filter rule could not.
sections.eli5: The old way was to write rules as a sentence of free text, which is easy to get wrong. The new way is a form with labeled boxes, so every computer fills it in and reads it the same way.

sections.title: Rule Sets and Rules
sections.content:
The top-level element is the QoS-Resources AVP (code 508), a Grouped AVP that holds one or more Filter-Rule AVPs (code 509). Each Filter-Rule pairs a condition with an action.

A rule can carry a Filter-Rule-Precedence AVP (code 510). A lower number means higher precedence, and rules with equal precedence MAY be executed in parallel if the Resource Management Function supports it. Without the AVP, rules SHOULD run in the order they appear in QoS-Resources.

If a rule has no QoS-Profile-Template and its action is shape or mark, the default applies: Vendor-Id 0 (the IETF) and QoS-Profile-Id 0, the profile defined in RFC 5624. The contents of QoS-Parameters are defined by whichever specification defines the profile.
sections.eli5: A rule book is a stack of rules. Each rule says when it applies and what to do. A number on each rule says which one goes first.

sections.title: Traffic Classifiers
sections.content:
A classifier says how to pick out a subset of packets. The Classifier AVP (code 511) must contain exactly one Classifier-ID and may contain a Protocol, a Direction, any number of From-Spec and To-Spec AVPs, and header options for IP, TCP, ICMP and Ethernet.

The model has a managed terminal, a Classifying Entity in the middle and unmanaged terminals beyond it. Direction is IN (0, from the managed terminal), OUT (1, to the managed terminal) or BOTH (2); if omitted, both directions match. In the IN and BOTH directions, From-Spec refers to the managed terminal and To-Spec to the unmanaged one. In OUT it is the reverse.

Addresses can be given as a single IP address, an inclusive range, or a base address with a mask width (the RFC's example is 192.0.2.0/24). Layer 2 matching uses MAC-48 or EUI-64 addresses, optionally with a mask pattern. Ports can be single or a range, where an omitted start means 0 and an omitted end means 65535. Use-Assigned-Address stands for the address given to the managed terminal when the AAA server does not know it yet.

Matching rules combine in a fixed way. Several instances of the same kind of AVP in one spec match if any one matches. IP address, MAC address and port AVPs in the same spec must all match. The Negated AVP inverts address matching but not port comparison.

Other options match the DiffServ code point, fragmentation flags (DF or MF), IP and TCP options, TCP flags, ICMP type and code, Ethernet type or SAP, VLAN-ID ranges (0 to 4095) for single or stacked tags, and 802.1D user priority (0 to 7).
sections.eli5: A classifier is a description of which packages to pick: from this street, to that house, shipped this way. You can also say everything except that street.

sections.title: Time-of-Day Conditions
sections.content:
A rule can also depend on the clock. The Time-Of-Day-Condition AVP (code 560) describes one time window. If a rule has several, the current time must fall inside at least one. If a rule has both a classifier and a time condition, both MUST match before the action applies.

A window is built from the start and end in seconds from midnight (0 to 86400), bit masks for the day of the week, day of the month and month of the year, and optional absolute start and end times counted in seconds since January 1, 1900, 00:00 UTC. Missing parts mean no restriction.

The Timezone-Flag says how to read the window: UTC (0, the default), LOCAL (1, local time at the managed terminal) or OFFSET (2). With OFFSET, the Timezone-Offset AVP MUST be present, in the range -43200 to 43200 seconds.
sections.eli5: You can also say this rule only works on weekdays from nine to five, like a shop's opening hours.

sections.title: Actions, QoS Semantics and Capability
sections.content:
The Treatment-Action AVP (code 572) says what happens to matching traffic: drop (0) MUST discard it, permit (3) lets it through, shape (1) delays packets to fit a profile, and mark (2) sets the DS codepoint. For shape and mark, the QoS-Parameters AVP SHALL carry the details, such as the TMOD-1 and Bandwidth AVPs or the PHB-Class AVP from RFC 5624.

The QoS-Profile-Template AVP names the profile with a vendor ID (an IANA Private Enterprise Number; 0 means the IETF) and a profile ID. Excess-Treatment says what happens to out-of-profile traffic. Policing is modeled by giving it an action of drop. If it is absent, the node doing the QoS treatment decides.

The QoS-Semantics AVP says what a rule's QoS means: QoS-Desired (0), QoS-Available (1), QoS-Delivered (2), Minimum-QoS (3) or QoS-Authorized (4). The meaning depends on direction. For example, a client sends QoS-Desired to request authorization, and the server answers with QoS-Authorized.

Finally, QoS-Capability (code 578) lists the profile templates a peer supports. It can announce capabilities or negotiate a common set; handling a failed negotiation is left to the application or deployment.
sections.eli5: Once a rule picks its packages, the action says what to do: throw them away, let them pass, slow them to a steady pace, or stamp them with a priority sticker.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows the AVPs inside ordinary Diameter exchanges. In Diameter EAP and NASREQ, the access server announces QoS-Capability, and the final answer carries QoS-Resources with QoS-Authorized for a pre-provisioned profile. In an authorization-only flow, the server is sent QoS-Desired and replies with QoS-Authorized or rejects it. A server can also start re-authorization with a Re-Auth Request, and the access server then re-requests.

In Diameter Credit Control, the client asks for QoS in the first Credit Control Request, the server grants it in the answer, and at the end of service the client reports the QoS actually delivered with QoS-Delivered.

The classifier examples include matching TCP traffic from the 192.0.2.0/24 subnet to three web servers and three ports, and matching UDP SIP signaling from one MAC address. A QoS example limits traffic to 1 Mbit/s with shape and drops the excess. Another marks in-profile traffic of 5 Mbit/s with one PHB class and the excess with a different class.
sections.eli5: The examples show the labels in real conversations. For instance, a customer asks for fast delivery, the shop says yes, and afterwards reports how fast it really was.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated AVP codes 508 through 578 from the Diameter AVP Codes registry for the AVPs in this document, from QoS-Resources (508) to QoS-Capability (578).

It also created two registries under the AAA parameters: one for QoS-Semantics values (0 to 4) and one for Treatment-Action values (0 to 3). New values in both are subject to the Specification Required policy from RFC 5226.
sections.eli5: The number registry is like a phone book. Each new label gets its own number so nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is short. It notes that the document extends Diameter to carry QoS information and points to the security discussion in the Diameter base protocol, RFC 3588. Use of these AVPs MUST take into account the security issues and requirements of the base protocol. The RFC adds no new security mechanism of its own.
sections.eli5: These labels ride inside Diameter, so they are protected the same way Diameter already protects its messages.

items.desc: Counterpart of drop; lets matching traffic bypass.
